title: Instrumental case
blurb: Say how you travel or what you use (no preposition needed), who you're with using s/se, and use the instrumental after stát se and zabývat se.

vocab.example: O víkendu jsem byl s rodinou.
Ve volném čase se zabývám hudbou.

grammarNote.title: Instrumental: means, „with“, and after stát se / zabývat se
grammarNote.text: The instrumental case answers "by/with what" and "with whom." It shows up in three everyday patterns. First, means or instrument — how you do something or get somewhere, with no preposition needed: jedu vlakem (I go by train), píšu perem (I write with a pen). Second, accompaniment after the preposition s/se (with): jdu s kamarádem, byl jsem s rodinou — s always takes the instrumental, just like bez always takes the genitive. Third, a handful of verbs pair with instrumental instead of accusative: stát se (to become) — stal se lékařem, "he became a doctor" — and zabývat se (to be occupied with) — zabývám se hudbou. Endings: masculine and neuter nouns add -em (bratr → bratrem, auto → autem); feminine -a nouns swap to -ou (žena → ženou); the question word kdo becomes kým in the instrumental (s kým? — with whom?).

check.prompt: How do you say "by train" in Czech (instrumental of vlak)?
check.explanation: Vlak is a masculine hard noun; the instrumental adds -em: vlakem.
check.note: Means of transport in the instrumental never needs a preposition: jedu vlakem, jedu autem, jedu autobusem.

check.prompt: The preposition „s“ (with) is always followed by the instrumental case.
check.explanation: Correct — s/se always takes the instrumental, whether it's accompaniment (s kamarádem) or a fixed phrase (co je s tebou?).
check.note: This pairs neatly with bez, which always takes the genitive — two prepositions, two fixed cases, no exceptions.

check.explanation: Lékař is a masculine noun; stát se pairs with the instrumental, so it becomes lékařem.

check.prompt: Change to instrumental: Jedu tam (autobus — bus). → Jedu tam ___.
check.explanation: Autobus is a masculine hard noun, so its instrumental form adds -em: autobusem.

title: A2 review & mini-check
blurb: A cumulative recap pulling together the accusative, past tense, future tense, and modal verbs from across A2.

vocab.example: Včera jsem byl unavený, tak jsem šel spát brzy.
Dnes ten úkol dělám, zítra ho udělám.

grammarNote.title: A2 in one page: cases, tense, aspect, and modals
grammarNote.text: Six building blocks came together across A2. Accusative marks the direct object (mám bratra, not mám bratr), and genitive covers possession, quantities, and a fixed set of prepositions like bez and z (bez cukru). Past tense uses the l-participle and agrees with the subject's gender — byl jsem unavený (male) vs. byla jsem unavená (female). Verb aspect splits every action into an ongoing/repeated imperfective (dělám) and a completed perfective (udělám) — a distinction English usually skips. Future tense either combines budu with an imperfective infinitive (budu pracovat) or simply uses the perfective present form to mean "will" (udělám = I will do it). And the four modals — muset (must), moct (can/may), chtít (want), smět (be allowed) — all pair directly with an infinitive: musím jít, můžu pomoct, chtěl bych kávu. With these in place, B1 opens with the last core case, dative, followed by a single lesson mapping all seven cases side by side.

check.prompt: Which sentence correctly says "I have a sister" using the accusative case?
check.explanation: Sestra is a feminine -a noun; as the direct object of mám it takes the accusative ending -u: sestru.
check.note: Recap from the accusative case lesson — the direct object always shifts out of the plain dictionary (nominative) form.

check.prompt: „Byla jsem unavená“ means the speaker is female.
check.explanation: Byla and unavená are both feminine past-tense/adjective forms — a male speaker would say byl jsem unavený.
check.note: Recap from the past tense lesson — the l-participle and adjective endings both track the subject's gender.

check.prompt: Zítra ___ pracovat. (I will work — budu + infinitive)
check.explanation: Budu plus an imperfective infinitive is the standard way to build the future tense for ongoing or repeated actions.

check.prompt: Turn this from "I have to go" into "you (informal, ty) have to go": „Musím jít.“ → „___ jít.“
check.explanation: Musíš is the ty-form of muset — modal verbs conjugate like any other verb and still pair with an infinitive.

title: Dative case
blurb: The last core case: mark who receives an action with giving/telling verbs, and use Czech's reversed „líbí se mi“ (I like it) construction.

vocab.translation: I like it. (lit. it pleases me)
vocab.example: Ten film se mi moc líbí.

grammarNote.title: Dative: the „to/for someone“ case, giving verbs, and líbí se mi
grammarNote.text: The dative case answers "to/for whom." It marks the indirect object — the receiver of an action — with giving and telling verbs: dát (to give), říct (to tell), napsat (to write to someone), volat (to call someone): dám ti dárek, volám mamince. It also drives Czech's "impersonal liking" constructions, where the thing liked is the grammatical subject and the person is in the dative: líbí se mi ten film literally means "that film is pleasing to me," and chutná mi ta polévka works the same way for taste. A handful of prepositions take dative too, especially k (to, towards) and kvůli (because of): kvůli tobě. Personal pronouns have their own dative forms worth memorizing directly: mi/mně (me), ti/tobě (you), mu/jemu (him), jí (her), nám (us), vám (you-formal/plural), jim (them). For nouns, masculine people-words usually take -ovi (bratr → bratrovi), neuter -o nouns take -u (auto → autu), and feminine -a nouns swap to -ě or -i with a consonant softening (matka → matce, Praha → Praze).

check.prompt: How do you say "I'll help you" (informal ty) in Czech using the dative pronoun?
check.explanation: Ti is the dative form of ty, used after pomoct — you help "to" someone, so the pronoun takes the dative, not the accusative.
check.note: Verbs like pomoct (help), věřit (trust), and rozumět (understand) all pair with the dative, not the accusative — worth learning as a fixed list.

check.prompt: „Líbí se mi ten film“ literally means the film is pleasing to me, with „mi“ as the dative pronoun for "to me."
check.explanation: Correct — Czech flips the English "I like the film" so the film is the subject and „mi“ (to me) is the dative experiencer.
check.note: Chutná mi (it tastes good to me) and hodí se mi (it suits me) work the same reversed way.

check.prompt: Dej ___ dárek. (give her a gift — dative of ona)
check.explanation: Jí is the dative form of ona ("she"), used for the person receiving the gift.

check.prompt: Change to dative: Volám (matka — mother). → Volám ___.
check.explanation: Matka is a feminine -a noun; in the dative singular the k softens to c: matce (like Praha → Praze).
